props.title: Foreign Correspondent
props.initialSlug: Reporter uncovers spy ring on eve of WWII

sections.content: Foreign Correspondent marks one of Hitchcock's earliest American triumphs, arriving the same year as Rebecca (1940). Shot while Europe descended into WWII, it's a masterclass in combining propaganda with entertainment. The film follows American reporter Johnny Jones (Joel McCrea) as he uncovers a Nazi spy ring in Britain, featuring some of Hitchcock's most innovative set pieces - including the iconic windmill sequence and a stunning plane crash into the Atlantic shot using revolutionary effects techniques. The film's closing speech, delivered as London faces Nazi bombing, served as a direct call to still-neutral America to join the war effort.

movies.title: Confessions of a Nazi Spy
movies.slug: The first major Hollywood anti-Nazi film, following an FBI agent investigating German spies in America

sections.content: Hitchcock's pre-war spy thrillers established templates that influenced decades of espionage cinema. The 39 Steps (1935) introduced the "wrong man" chase format, while Saboteur (1942) perfected it for American audiences. Foreign Correspondent sits perfectly between them, combining European-style paranoia with Hollywood production values. The film's influence echoes through later works like North by Northwest (1959) and even modern thrillers like Bridge of Spies (2015). SUBHEAD: Wartime Propaganda & Entertainment

The film's remarkable achievement is making anti-fascist propaganda thrilling entertainment. Unlike heavy-handed contemporary films like Mrs. Miniver (1942), Hitchcock wraps his message in masterful suspense sequences. The assassination in the rain using umbrellas, the windmill's mysterious rotating blades, and the harrowing plane crash finale remain stunning technical achievements. These sequences influenced countless later films, from The Third Man (1949) to Three Days of the Condor (1975).
